activity_context.topic_title: The Second Derivative of a Multivariable Function

examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Second Derivative of a Function
examples.problem: Find $\boldsymbol f''(1,0)$ for the function $f(x,y)  = x^2 e^y.$
examples.worked_solution:
For a function $f: \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R,$ given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070131/assets/7444a8128c085d7bf4f56a57a60c260864a50da0b744b6dbe22a2ced89a0588d.png)

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070131/assets/22dd960829ea268e5aade685b56949f8998f87ae8c040a90f04436cbfc6b9a58.png)

In our case, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070131/assets/4fede2bb5c2306f62b55b7996488baee52c69e7d41b011e0e9d2b7405e63a8f4.png)

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{e}^{y}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{e}^{y})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x{e}^{y} & {x}^{2}{e}^{y}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x\text{ }\,{e}^{y})=2\text{ }\,{e}^{y}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{e}^{y})=2x\text{ }\,{e}^{y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x\text{ }\,{e}^{y})=2x\text{ }\,{e}^{y}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{e}^{y})={x}^{2}{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}2\text{ }\,{e}^{y} & 2x\text{ }\,{e}^{y} \\ 2x\text{ }\,{e}^{y} & {x}^{2}{e}^{y}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate this matrix at $\left(1,0\right).$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,0)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Find ${f}^{″}(2,\frac{\pi }{2})$ for the function $f(x,y)$ given that
${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y & {x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{aligned}]$
feedback.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y & {x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{aligned}],$ 
 we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=-{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡y & 2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ 2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y & -{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate this matrix at $(2,\frac{\pi }{2}).$ This gives

$$
{f}^{″}(2,\frac{\pi }{2})=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$
